utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Senior trial attorney Mr. Grant Niemann continues to be out of the country. I'm here, Teresa McHenry, with co-counsel Giuliano Turone and our case manager, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I am defending Mr. Delalic, and with me is Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. With me defending Mr. Mucic is Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic. I am representing Mr. Hazim Delic. With me is Mr. Thomas Moran, lawyer from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman representing Esad Landzo. With me is Cynthia McMurrey from Houston. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still testifying under oath. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. Thank you. I should just like to check my headphones, because my colleague tells me that there are some difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can proceed, please, if you are ready. You have difficulties? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I can't hear anything. (Pause). Yes, I can hear now. Thank you. Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Good morning, Mr. P. As you have heard, I'm Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. P, I should just like to draw to your attention, as well as mine, that you were testifying all day yesterday by answering questions put to you by persons who were not speaking our language. The two of us can understand each other well so that we could probably have this conversation at quite a fast pace, but I would like to ask you to wait and listen for the translation, which I must do also, otherwise the Trial Chamber and all others here present will not be able to follow. Do we understand one another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. P, prior to this hearing you asked for protective measures for reasons which were accepted by the court; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on in the media and elsewhere you had spoken about the situation you were in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the newspaper Telegraf of 6th March 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that article in the Telegraf various persons and officials were mentioned from Konjic and Bosnia-Herzegovina from that period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, various names were mentioned, but there are at least 20 newspapers coming out in Belgrade daily, and in each of those newspapers you can read a different interpretation of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but you didn't read that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read the Telegraf somewhere in mid-April, when I returned from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Zejnil Delalic's name was not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In any case, Mr. P, you lived in Konjic for years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not personally know Mr. Delalic before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I met Mr. Delalic once. I was introduced to him at my colleague's place, Dr. Jusufbegovic's. That was on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that Mr. Delalic lived abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also knew, as you testified before this Trial Chamber, that he came to Konjic occasionally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have now mentioned your meeting with Mr. Delalic in your medical centre, you certainly know that Mr. Delalic was a friend of your director, Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a very good friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that Mr. Delalic was very well acquainted with some of your colleagues, for instance Dr. Grubac, but some others as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That friendship was linked to both the treatment of members of his family, but it went beyond that; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you were introduced to Mr. Delalic just before the war in the hospital, I'm sure that you must know as a doctor, and please confirm this for me, that Mr. Delalic had just before the war provided this hospital with two haemodialysis devices, but that that equipment had still not been installed because of some technical problems with the building itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there were two of these devices for haemodialysis and personnel were sent for training to the dialysis centre in Elija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the donator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Being a doctor, you also probably know that a number of patients from Konjic had to go for haemodialysis once or twice a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you also know that they were taken for haemodialysis to Sarajevo; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, but I think that just because of the war, because there were too many patients, one of them was driven to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can tell me what happens with patients who depend on these haemodialysis devices, if this is not carried out on time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he skips two or three of these treatments, it means that they are heading straight towards death.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The patients from Konjic you drove with your ambulance -- I'm thinking of your medical centre that took them there for treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And those patients on the way to Sarajevo had to pass through Bradina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, like other people, you can confirm that Bradina is on the M17 highway linking Konjic to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the number of the highway, but I do know that it links Sarajevo to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably don't know the number, but you know that it is the only main asphalt road between those towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know there are other roundabout ways, but I think it's the only asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you can confirm that, in the event that this route is blocked, normal communication between Konjic and Sarajevo becomes impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except roundabout -- using roundabout routes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you stated that, as a specialist, an ear, nose and throat specialist, under certain conditions and for certain reasons you left the medical centre in Konjic and went to Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, this happened on 24th or 25th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your family was already there; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They left that day, only they went by bus, and I came by car. As they were taken off the bus at the checkpoint in Podorasac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said that there was a checkpoint in Podorasac where the reserve police force of the Konjic police was stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that when you returned to Konjic, you received a telephone call and you learned that a group of Muslims who wanted to leave the territory of Konjic had been stopped at the barricade in Bradina. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. P, you knew and you later saw that there were barricades in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a control checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That checkpoint was not set up by the police, nor the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Mr. P, as you testified before this court, until May 4th or 5th you travelled to Konjic to work with some interruptions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 5th or 6th May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you can then recall that on May 1st, 1992 your director, Dr. Jusufbegovic, accompanied two ambulances carrying patients for haemodialysis going to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in response to my request.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that, precisely because you had called them, they were stopped on the road at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with Dr. Jusufbegovic was Dr. Risto Kalen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then after six years (sic) of negotiations with persons at this checkpoint you managed to ensure -- after six hours of talks you managed to achieve that these passengers were allowed to pass through to go to Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tunnel had caved in on the side towards the Vukovici village where the Muslims were. It was not possible to pass by car. They returned to Bradina. They looked me up. I went to see what was happening. I found this tunnel caved in, in the sense of a truckload of earth had been piled up, and they asked the workers to remove this earth so that the ambulance could pass. Then I said that the situation was tense, to which Dr. Risto Kalen's comment was: "Give them something to drink." Then a verbal discussion started, and I nearly had a fight with him, because I did not agree with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. P. You explained that thanks to your efforts this was the last transport of persons going for dialysis to pass through Bradina before the fighting broke out, as you were saying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was possible to pass through once again, because the tunnel was hit again from the same side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. P, after that you stayed in Bradina in the local outpatients' clinic in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until there were telephone lines, I informed my director every morning of where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, as you had stated, the decision to stay there was discussed -- you discussed this decision with your superior, Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it is more correct to say, Mr. P, that this conversation was carried out in your presence with Dr. Jusufbegovic by Dr. Grubac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Dr. Jusufbegovic went to his native village, Repovci, which is a Muslim village, and to get there he has to pass by my house. We sat in front of my house and I told him: "I'll come to work regularly for as long as there is any transport".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you explained this to us yesterday. So you don't know anything about the telephone conversation that your colleague had with Dr. Jusufbegovic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, your family, which was in Bradina, was later transferred to Hadici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was actually about ten days after you had come to Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They went to Hadici to stay with your uncle, Milos Mrkajic, because you felt they would be safer there, as Hadici in those days was under the control of the JNA and the Serb forces; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My uncle had an older son, who lived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Cacik, and I felt that from there it would be easiest for them to reach safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that somewhere around 20th April about 200 HOS members arrived in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that they were first stationed at the Konjic motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that their appearance provoked fear in the town among the ordinary people so that people started to flee the city, both Serbs and Muslims; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Only may I add --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain to me what a HOS means and do you know where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but it means the Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to work for the last time to Konjic on 5th or 6th May, the town had been shelled already on 4th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to work to Konjic and the town was shelled. You could see some broken glass in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know, Mr. P, that the shelling came from the eastern side, from the direction of Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistic expert, nor am I a soldier. All I can say is that there was shelling, there was broken glass and damage to the fronts of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know, Mr. P, that on 17th April in Konjic a general mobilisation had been proclaimed because of the immediate threat of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that all able-bodied men were virtually prohibited from leaving town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know, or at least I think you do, so please confirm this, that the HOS soldiers who were in the motel later moved to Podorasac, a place between Konjic and Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear of that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, did you know that in Podorasac the HVO command was situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the commander of the HVO in that region was Zovko Zvonko, or at least he was referred to as such, Zvonko Zovko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander. I did see Zvonko when I was stopped at the checkpoint in Podorasac wearing a camouflage uniform in a vehicle make Lada Niva, the property of the Sipad company from Konjic, and when I reached Mr. Delalic's on 27th, I found in the apartment Mr. Dinko Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have already told us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to add something. And I assumed he was the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Dinko Zebic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated before the Trial Chamber that you had no official or political function and that, in fact, you did not engage in politics in those days; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In a report submitted by the Prosecutor to the defence there are some data which I should like you to tell me whether they are true or not, namely is it true that while you were in Bradina you had tried to use your influence to prevent the conflict from flaring up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in April 1992 you took part in the first meeting held in Pero Mrkajic's cafe in Bradina, which was attended from the Serbian side by Kuljanin Jovo, Mrkajic Pero, Gligorevic Radovan? This was from your side, the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other people too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But these people were there, weren't they, and do you remember who were the negotiators on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Ajanovic Fikret. We called him "Fiko". He graduated in mechanical engineering and he was working in Sarajevo. I knew the other people except for one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the second meeting was held in Sunje at the beginning of May and it was attended on the Serb side by Jovo Kuljanin, Branoslav Gligorevic, yourself and Vaso Vujicic Kisa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who attended then on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Saban Spiljak, Ljevo -- I can't remember his first name -- his father, and I do not recall the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The third meeting was held in the village of Zukici, and on the Serbian side present were Vujicic Vaso, Rajko, you, Mr. P, and Jovo Kuljanin. This meeting was held in mid-May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was another representative present as well. I think you forgot him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you can recall him, you can mention him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who your interlocutors were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Lokas, Mr. Smajo Prevljak, and I can't recall the name -- Diver. He was a military officer on active duty, and then he asked me whether I was a representative of any military authorities, and I answered that I was not, that had I wanted to be a soldier, I would have been that a long time ago and I would have had a much higher rank than he did. I state now whenever I went to those negotiations I was waited upon after my shift in the dispensary because people trusted me. I knew a lot of people, and they were certain that nothing will happen to them if I was there with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was a fourth meeting, which was attended on your side by the same persons that you mentioned and on the other side, except for Diver, there was also Ahmed Jusufbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that meeting at all, and I don't recall at all that I met Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, when defence counsel refers to a report submitted by the prosecution, it was just a report given as part of discovery, not necessarily a report prepared by the prosecution and not provided as something that was or was not accurate. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I am just trying to ascertain the facts, because Mr. P was talking about his engagement up there, and I wanted to hear him state that himself, so this was just an opportunity for me to check the facts. I'm not interested in the report per se. Mr. P has really given us a comprehensive account of what was going on up there. So, Mr. P, since you have stated the positions of some of your interlocutors, could you please tell us who Mr. Goran Lokas was? You did not tell us much about him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Goran Lokas as the President of the municipal court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time did he take part in negotiations as President of the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot speak to that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, can you tell me whether at those meetings the discussion was also held about surrendering of arms and removal of barricades from the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The discussion was about not attacking and free movement of goods and people. It was agreed that anything could pass through, both people and goods, but no arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. P, you know that until 25th May the free traffic, free passage, was not secured; in other words, barricades were not dismantled, and the weapons were not turned in by the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was agreed when I was last there on 25th May at 12 o'clock that there will be additional negotiations in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would please like you to answer me the following question: regardless of what was agreed, on that day, by that day, no barricades were dismantled or weapons turned in; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days before 25th May some women started down to Konjic, because no -- there was no bus transportation from Repovci, going through Bradina towards Konjic. So they came to this caved-in tunnel on the south side of the tunnel, which had been caved in by the HVO and the TO forces, as far as I know. At the bridge they were met. Niksic -- I don't recall his first name -- and he was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know you know a lot about events there, but my question is whether the arms, the weapons had been turned in, surrendered. If you know that, please say so or if you don't, please say so, so that we wouldn't expand on this story. Do you know whether the barricades were removed by 25th May and whether the population had turned in the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please do not try to simplify the matters. Let's go in order, but I will answer your question: no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated before this Trial Chamber that because of fear and other reasons the population organised self-defence, so you knew that people were acquiring weapons in case of necessity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The black market for weapons, for oil and cigarettes was active.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, Mr. P, you knew that, as you said it, after sporadic conflicts on the line of separation trenches were also being dug around Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of that. I did not go to those places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of these combat operations in Bradina you stated that you were in the dispensary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the afternoon Radovan Kuljanin arrived at the dispensary and he had a bullet wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You treated him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nedjo Kuljanin's father came to you later that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nedjo Kuljanin had a wound on his right upper leg and you went to Suljina Strana to treat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After this you returned to the dispensary, where you spent the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, together with Milan Zuza, Milovan Kuljanin, Risto Mrkajic, Kuljanin Radovan, you surrendered to the members of the HVO and TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not in the morning; it was 4 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was 26th May at 4 o'clock in the afternoon. Mr. P, even though the population was arming itself, as you stated, you personally had no weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some time in mid-May, Drago Vujicic, called Spaco, did offer you a weapon but you refused it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that your colleague, Dr. Milan Zuza, at the time of your arrest, turned over his automatic rifle to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He kept this rifle in this dispensary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the dentistry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you stated, you were arrested together with another 100-150 persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However,, when you started on foot and then later in that truck, those were exclusively men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Children and women stayed in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for restating that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the arrested people, and Dr. Zuza was one of them, surrendered their weapons right away, and some others either threw it away or hid it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that out; I learned that in the prison that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the Trial Chamber you described in some detail the tortures that you suffered in Bradina. As a human being I feel very sorry for what happened to you, but I need to ask several additional questions relating to that. You were taken to Musala Sports Hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I'm not sure how precise your answer was on that issue. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't have been precise, because I cannot tell exactly. I think that we were kept 30-40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. P, you were told at that time that you were brought there by mistake, and that you should have been taken to Grude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is Grude, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a Croatian town in the present day -- in the present territory of Herceg-Bosna, which is part of the Croat Muslim Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you knew that the headquarters of the HVO was located there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, after all the mistreatment that you suffered, you were brought to Celebici and you were taken to the underground tunnel together with other arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the torture that accompanied this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know the time -- what time it was when you were brought to this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was around 3.00, 3.30 in the morning of 27th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it's in the night between 26th and 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your group was also an elderly man Mirko Kuljanin from Bradina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him. I could give you some names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could, yes, two or three please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones that I remember are Milan Zuza, Mijailo Mrkajic, Relja Kuljanin, Radomir Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That's sufficient. Thank you. You stated that at some point Miralem Musinovic, called Rale, appeared and he introduced himself as the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How much time did elapse between the time you were brought to the tunnel and the time that Rale Musinovic came to call you to come out of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether at that time other persons were also taken out of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the first to be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you recall that at that time Simo Jovanovic and his brother were also taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I only know that I was brought out first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you stated that at that time some individuals were waiting for you there. Could you tell us what those -- who those individuals were and what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- they were Marko Rajic, the driver, who used to work in the Unis company in Konjic, and it seems to me there were two additional persons present there, of whom I think one's name was Gulas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what duties they had, what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you were brought out where did you go first on that early morning of 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was first allowed to find my shoes on the heap of shoes and then they took me to Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some time around 4 o'clock in the morning, as you confirmed, you were brought to the house of Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise you knew that Mr. Delalic had a house in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was well-known to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that this house is located at the exit of Konjic towards Celebici and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, across from the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This house has a ground floor and a top floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Looking towards Celebici on the left-hand side, this is where this highway which was called M17 passes, right by the house, by the fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Across from this house is the gas station that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this gas station -- both this gas station and Mr. Delalic's house are sort of located under a very large rock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the river Neretva runs by the house and one could say this is where the Jablanica lake starts, because that's where it starts widening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There's a lot of greenery and woods and trees surrounding that area; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not pass by there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that in the ground floor of the house there was a disco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, when you came, you were taken to the top floor, where there was the apartment of Mr. Delalic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now, and we will ask the Technical Department for help, to help me locate -- identify the location. The prosecution has viewed this tape and I would like the tape number 1 shown. I think there is probably no objection on the part of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct. I was given this videotape yesterday and have seen it. No objection. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Please could the witness be shown the tape number 1, and since there's no audio on it, I don't think that -- we don't need to go into private session or anything. We can just show it as is. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the gas station that you mentioned; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell the Yugopetrol sign there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the fence of the house towards the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm better oriented with models. You'll see next to the gas station --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the site towards the motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This seems to be the house of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The entire tape is just about four minutes long, so at the end you can comment. This is the entrance to the disco. Perhaps there are some changes here, because the tape is recent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall we discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just see the entire tape. I would like you to -- I would just like to know whether you recognise the house or not. You entered -- you probably entered from the other side, and this is the side facing the motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered from the other side. I don't see the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's from the other side. This was just shot from this side. You'll see -- you can see the gas station from here. You'll see it in close-up. Neretva is over on that side; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still can't see the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The stairs are on the other side, but is this Mr. Delalic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess probably but I can't see the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But this is the entrance to the disco. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- yes, I see. There was the carwash place and the car mechanics and then also the video games for children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you where you entered, because obviously the stairs are from the other side, but on this video you can recognise Mr. Delalic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only confirm it by the side for where the stairs are, so I'm just telling you what I'm sure about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would just like this marked for identification, and when somebody is able to recognise the house, then we will offer it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can make you a drawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks. That will not be necessary. Since you did not -- this is the -- so this is the house which you did not fully recognise; this is the house you were brought into on 27th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Together with you, who else entered this house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Could I have an explanation about what kind of thing is a disco? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): A disco is a night gathering place mostly for the youth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): That's what it was before the war. This is what these premises were before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. You said who entered first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Marko Ruzic. I waited a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you entered, you said that Mr. Delalic was wearing a morning robe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, please let's have a break and come back at 12. We will come back at 12. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 noon)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, I think you can proceed please. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Mr. P, to go back to the point where we were before the break, you were called out and taken out of Tunnel Number 9 by Mr. Rale Musinovic; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you left the tunnel and when Rale told you that you had to go and do your job, you were not tied up at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your bloodstained coat you sat in the car. You were not tied up then either, or in the position of somebody who was being arrested. You were not tied up in the car, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is how you entered Mr. Delalic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, when Rale told you this, you understood that you were being released from the tunnel; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How was I supposed to know, because I didn't know where he was taking me? He just said that I was going to work, but I didn't know where he was taking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Early on and in answer to my question you already explained that you reached Mr. Delalic's house, that he was wearing his robe. He offered you something to eat and to drink; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: in addition to Zebic, who else was in this room where you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A woman was coming in. I don't know her name or surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the conversation -- then you washed up, then you had coffee, and in the meantime it had dawned, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic and Mr. Zebic told you that they were sure that you had not participated in the conflict in Bradina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm quoting now. "According to our knowledge, at present you sought to calm down the situation". Mr. Zebic asked me whether I knew Mrs. Stojka Boras. I answered "yes".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the question, please. You had already told some local people in Bradina that they should not insult Mrs. Boras; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't Mr. Delalic tell you then that he would try to take you back to the hospital in collaboration with your director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then he called up Mr. Jusufbegovic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. P, will you tell me when -- a previous question first. You knew that the town had been shelled on the last day that you were there, that the shelling continued, that there was a lot of talk about what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and, this is my question: at the time there was -- anti-Serbian feeling was rampant in the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then and a little later you could feel that you were being avoided by your close friends even?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't even refrain from allowing me to be slapped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also knew that the Croats and Muslims at the time in such an atmosphere, who had tried to help some Serbs, that they were highly criticised in town and some were even accused of collaborating with the Cetniks; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called them the fifth column.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you knew at the time that there were few people who dared to help those people, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, there were people who paid no attention to such prejudices and to their personal safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very few such people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us go back to this trip you made from the hospital, where your injuries were treated, to Celebici. You said that you spent two days at the Gynaecology Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the night, I spent the day, I spent the next night and until the following day, about 3 o'clock I was transferred together I think with two or three other injured people, who had plaster extensions. I'm not quite sure on which legs they had plaster, and on their hips -- the upper leg and hip.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you spent those two days there as a patient, not as a doctor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not absolutely right, because on the temperature chart it was noted "SE, KS, urine, RTG, pulmo, RTO, craniogram".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that would mean what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of these tests were carried out. I just received one infusion and I was given an analgesic intramuscular, an injection.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not acting as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were in a room with other patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were not under guard protection. Some uniformed men would come in occasionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you were transferred to the Third of March School, which was an improvised infirmary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was inadequate as accommodation. There was just a desk, a teacher's desk, a classroom desk, on which we held the drum and the instruments I had already indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you went there as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told I was going there as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This school is close to the hospital, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Both the school and the hospital were at a spot that was exposed to combat operations, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume so. I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With your colleagues, Grubac and Zuza, you treated the injured detainees, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just answered my question. Some of the prisoners who had serious injuries received medical treatment in the hospital where you were too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Marko Mrkajic, Sejad Gligorevic and some others whose names I cannot recall just now, but, madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't ask me anything. That is not the situation, so will you just please answer my questions? Thank you. Maybe on some other occasion. Is it true that when you reach that school, that must have been somewhere around 30th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, and you came across another 25 patients in the school already, whose wounds had been treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later the number, as you said, increased to about 30; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were in that school with those patients all the time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were able to go out into town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under no circumstances. How could I go out? The police was standing in front of the door. We had to knock when we wanted to use the toilet. We were allowed to do that twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually the school was guarded by members of the Konjic police; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first couple of days members of the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then later Konjic police as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know any members of the MUP. These were civilians who had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also confirmed in this Trial Chamber that Slobodan Babic from Donje Selo died in that school; is that so? You just established his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Babic comes from the village of Bijelovcina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But that is the region of Donje Selo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that I established his death.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. After some ten days or so for security reasons, as you were told, you were transferred with some of the injured patients to the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that did Mr. Jusufbegovic tell you that your colleagues were not willing to agree to your working with them in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival in Celebici and Building Number 22 you actually had no insight into what was happening in town and within the territory of the Konjic municipality; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you would know if a new group was to be brought into the prison; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would learn of something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: do you know that somewhere around the beginning of June, the first week of June, a group of Serbs was brought in who had been -- from Bradina, who had been arrested at Mount Igman and who had tried to escape across Mount Igman to Kalinovic. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know that it was said that this was a group of radical Serbs and upon their arrest they were severely beaten up; is that so? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were killed and some were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that within this group was your relative Pero Mrkajic, who had also been heavily beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already explained to the Trial Chamber that due to these injuries Pero died. You spoke about this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just ask, so the record is clear -- I'm not objecting -- to clarify whether or not there is more than one Pero Mrkajic and which we are talking about, since I believe there may be more than one, just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She's talking about his relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, but when the witness is referring -- I just think we need to clarify exactly where this person was when he died, just so the record is clear about who we are talking about. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Very well. I'll try to clear this up. Therefore, the group which after the first week of June was arrested and detained and beaten up in the process, and that arrived at the Celebici camp, was the group which included your relative Pero Mrkajic that you said yesterday had died; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two Pero Mrkajics. There was the one from Musala. There was little Pero, known as "Little Pero", and big Pero. This was big Pero.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was -- he had a cafe and he died in Celebici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If certain persons made statements here and who were arrested with him and who said that he died in the first half of June, then it was an omission on your part when you said that this had happened at the end of June or the beginning of July. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Let us clear this up. We can talk about the period up to 22nd and the period after 22nd July. July, when I was released, because after five years, and every effort to forget and suppress into my subconscious all this, I cannot indicate the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. P, let us clear this up. You have a certain date which you remember, that is the period of your arrest, the period of your release and then the period after you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you would agree that in the period between your arrest and your release you cannot exactly remember all the dates and state with precision when an event took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. P, you stated that some prisoners who had been wounded during the shelling of Musala had been brought to Building 22; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were for a time the most serious patients you had in Building 22; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whose treatment took the longest time, two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Across the way from Building 22 there was the command building of the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of July a mixed team of investigators was working there, who took statements from the prisoners. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those investigators belonged to the MUP and the HVO. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the work of this Commission the President of the Commission was Goran Lokas; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned that in the Third of March elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, after early July you no longer saw those persons interrogating prisoners; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They interrogated -- the people who were interrogating were Miroslav Stenek; known as Kuvar, or the cook, somebody called Kuvar or the cook. I can't remember his name or surname. Pajic, a sergeant. I can't remember his name. Those were the people I knew among the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether we have understood one another well. They carried out interrogations until the beginning of July of that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly until when.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were personally interrogated, as you said, by Pajic. Let me remind you. His name is Sacir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his name. It is correct that his name was Pajic. I'm sorry. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew, Mr. P, that this Commission had the authority to decide who would be released and that at first some 50 persons were released more or less immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Persons started to be released, I think, on 3rd September, with the exception of Miro Golubovic, his father Stanko, myself and my colleague, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You made your statement, as you said, some ten days or ten to fifteen days after being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever you said has been taken down in the transcript -- was taken down during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic didn't use any force during the questioning; on the contrary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the contrary, he was very polite.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody punished you in any way during the interrogation, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. P, you said that that statement was about half an A4 format page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, since you said that you made such a statement, to look at this statement -- it is not a very good copy -- to try to see whether that is the statement you made in Celebici. I think we received this from the prosecutor, but anyway we have a copy here for the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It was not received from the prosecution and I would like to see it before it is shown to the witness. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes, here you are, please. Please show it to the prosecution. There's a copy for the Trial Chamber and for the witness. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would just ask, since this has not been given to the prosecution previously, for what purpose it is being offered to the witness? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): It is being offered to the witness to identify it as his statement, to identify this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I must object, because this is once again -- the prosecution has not been given this in advance, and, as we have told defence counsel in writing, we are going to object. We didn't object for the first part of the trial, but we've consistently asked for any evidence the defence intends to introduce. We were not given this, and therefore I would object:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have your reaction to that allegation? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): As I have pointed out a number of times, the obligation of the defence, according to Rule 66 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, is to give the Prosecutor all evidence that we have in our possession and which we intend to use as evidence. Since this is a document which we will be using as evidence only if the witness identifies it, we did not disclose it. We are not obliged to disclose it in accordance with Rule 66B to the prosecution. We have done so now, since the witness is here present, and he can identify whether it is the statement he made in Celebici on 8th July. This provision of the Rules is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is, the defence is not obliged to tender to the prosecution statements they intend to use. Is that very clear? They have no obligation to give to the prosecution a statement they intend to use? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): That is what I just said. I think that the Rule has -- the Trial Chamber has already ruled on this matter. Any document that we intend to use as evidence and which we have in our possession, we are obliged to give to the prosecution. 66B and 67 obliges us to do this, but, as we can use this as evidence only after it has been identified by the witness, we are still not proposing this, and therefore I think that as you and this Trial Chamber have agreed to such a procedure, that it should be submitted to the witness for identification, and only then tendered as evidence. If he does not identify it, then we cannot propose it as evidence. The witness has already testified many things related to this statement, virtually everything. I'm just interested in learning whether this is that statement of his, because I can ask him further questions on the basis of this statement before I can tender it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just briefly respond, with all due respect to my esteemed colleague, Ms. Residovic, I find this argument unbelievable, that the discovery rules, when they indicate that someone shall -- be it the prosecution or the defence -- intends to use evidence, what it means is: after the grounds for getting it admitted are established, then you show it to the prosecution. . This has come up on numerous occasions before, initially oftentimes because the particular document -- we didn't object to the particular document. We did not object, but we have made it very clear in the recent past that this is a clear violation, clear and continued violation of the rules of discovery. The prosecution has since the time of the first appearance been providing the defence with a large, large number of documents, identified what it intends to use as evidence, and the notion that -- what it means is that all you have to do is at the moment you show it to the witness give it to the prosecution makes a mockery out of the Rules of this Tribunal. I think this Chamber needs to make it very clear to the parties that giving the prosecution what it intends to use as evidence at the time they proffer it to the witness is absolutely unacceptable, and we must immediately be given all evidence which the defence intends to use as evidence. The defence did not have to choose to invoke the extensive discovery rules, which imposes upon them reciprocal discovery obligations. The defence did so. It was made very clear by this Trial Chamber, including the prior judges at the time the defence made this, that it did require the defence to give us those things, and therefore I would ask for a very clear ruling from this Tribunal that we must immediately be given all evidence that the defence intends to use throughout this -- throughout the prosecution case and throughout the defence case. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): The defence turned over all evidence that it intends to use to the prosecution, and also all the evidence that it is presenting during the proceedings it is also turning over. It is very clear what the Trial Chamber ruled on the need to turn over the witness list as well, but yesterday we found ourselves in a situation that we received very significant documents from the standpoint of a certain defence counsel, but we received these documents without the sources of these documents being listed. So I'm trying to strictly abide by Rule 66. The Delalic defence provided over 100 documents to the prosecution. Even this morning's videotape was provided to them. Rule 66 is very clear, the moment the defence has in its possession a piece of evidence and intends to present it. So the cumulative conditions are met, and the Trial Chamber agreed to this, and I am pursuing the same procedure: after this request by the prosecution, should the Trial Chamber come to a different decision, we will abide by that. We will comply with it, but we have to clarify it and make sure that these are the rules that apply to both the prosecution and to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are relying on which Rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The prosecution is relying on 67C: "If the defence makes a request pursuant to subrule 66B..." All the accused in this case made a request under Rule 66B. At the time they made the request the Trial Chamber -- it was the same Trial Chamber but different judges -- made it very clear on the record that the defence was doing this and that the defence understood that there were reciprocal discovery obligations as set out in this Rule, and we would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 67 is related to 66B.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If the defence had wanted to look at all the documents of the prosecution, so the prosecution has also a right to look at all the documents which the defence intends to use as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. There is no dispute here that the defence has invoked and taken advantage of Rule 66B from the beginning at great -- and the prosecution has spent hundreds, if not thousands, of hours complying with its discovery obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your contention is that there is reciprocity in every document which they intend to use.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am really not sure if I understand it, but I would certainly say that the defence is required to allow us to inspect all -- let's talk about this case -- all documents which are within their custody or control and which they intend to use as evidence at the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the provision 66B.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I'm sorry. I was reading from 67C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is related to 66B.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. 67C is applicable if the defence makes a request under 66B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The point is where does the reciprocity come, because if there is reciprocity, it should fall within those provisions, that having given notice under those provisions and being entitled to look through your documents, then you should be also entitled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I exactly understand your Honour. The prosecution is not here saying that the reciprocal obligations are identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that 66B, what the prosecution is required to do may be broader than what the defence is required to do, but the minimum -- there cannot be any argument that at the minimum the defence is required to provide us or allow us to inspect all documents which they intend to use as evidence at trial. That is the clear language of the Statute. I'm sorry -- the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Read what 66B says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. 66B states that: "The Prosecutor shall on request, subject to subrule C, permit the defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs and tangible objects in his custody or control, which are material to the preparation of the defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial, or were obtained from or belonged to the accused."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Now this enables you to invoke 67C.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct. The defence has taken full advantage of all provisions of Rule 66B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When they did this, the Trial Chamber confirmed in open court that they were doing this and that they understood that they had reciprocal discovery obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you actually invoked 67C?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We invoked it at the time and we have been continuing to press and have done so by letters as long as a year ago, by motions in this court. The Trial Chamber made it very clear, and I don't believe even the defence would disagree that we have consistently been asking for our rights under 67C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps there is some difficulty of interpretation. If what you are entitled to is limited to the documents listed in 67C, then it wouldn't extend to statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Your Honour, we are not -- I understand that there may well be another argument about whether or not the prosecution is entitled to defence witness statements, and the prosecution may well make that argument at another time. That is not the argument that we're making now. The argument that we are making now is: Ms. Residovic has indicated and stated that she intends to use this document as evidence in the trial, assuming the witness is able to recognise it, and therefore we believe that there cannot be any argument that the document falls within the clear meaning or the clear words of Rule 67C. It is a document which she intends to use as evidence in trial. The issue is: Ms. Residovic is stating that she wishes to use it at trial, but until the defence -- I'm sorry -- until the witness identifies it, she can't, and that therefore somehow the Rules don't apply, and I think this makes a mockery out of the Rules of the Tribunal. Such a ruling would apply both to the prosecution and the defence. In effect, it would get rid of the discovery obligations, because certainly you never know until you show a witness something whether or not -- and, in fact, until your Honours rule, you never know whether or not you will be successful in getting it, but ... I would just ask for a very clear direction, because Ms. Residovic has indicated that if -- she's willing to abide by this Chamber's Rule, and I have no idea how prejudiced we will be by the fact that we haven't clearly received some of this material in the past, but immediately the prosecution would be requesting a very clear order to the defence indicating that Rule 67C requires that they give us immediately all evidence that they intend at the present time to use at trial now in the prosecution case or in the defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I speak just very generally to this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do that not because I have any particular interest in the document that is in question now, but in the broader general rule that may arise as a result of your decision on this particular issue. Rule 66 I think if you read it contemplates that the defence makes a request of the prosecution, and, based upon that request, then the documents the prosecution has are turned over to the defence, creating a reciprocal obligation. The Prosecutor has not perhaps even as of today fully complied with those obligations. We just received this morning, and I haven't even had a chance to look at them, another whole stack of documents. Now I'm not complaining that the Prosecutor ought not to be giving us documents they should be giving us, but here we are, months and months into this case, and they are still giving us documents pursuant to our request under Rule 66. The second thing that concerns me, and that I'm mostly interested in, is this: there may very well be documents in the possession of the defendants that we don't have any present intention to offer into evidence, because we cannot know what a witness might testify to. That document may be all of a sudden, based on that witness's testimony, something that becomes relevant for the purposes of impeachment. I think Ms. McHenry understands that certain documents that you don't intend to use in evidence may be -- based upon the testimony may at that point become relevant for impeachment purposes. So we certainly couldn't be expected to turn over to the Prosecutor and they to us documents which they have no intention of using in evidence until such time as a witness testifies in such a way that makes that document relevant as an impeachment document, to impeach the testimony of that witness. So I guess I'm not disagreeing strongly with Ms. McHenry's position, but I only want to make it clear to the court that we reserve our right to use any document we may have for impeachment purposes if the witness testifies contrary to what we all might expect. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that your position even if you breach the obligations to provide documents reciprocally?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Rule, as I understand it, requires us to turn over documents we intend to use in evidence. I may have a document I have no intention of using in evidence. I have no intention of putting on a witness and putting that document in evidence through that witness. The documents that I intend to put on through the witnesses that I call either have been turned over or will be turned over as soon as they come into our possession. I think that's what the Rule speaks of, but when a prosecution witness takes the witness stand and testifies in an unexpected manner, and all of a sudden there is a document that we have in our possession that we never intended to use, that all of a sudden becomes relevant for impeachment of that witness, then I think we can use it without having had previously turned it over to the prosecution, because it's not a document that we intended to use in evidence in our case in chief. I know and I can absolutely assure you that the time will come when the defence case is going on that the prosecution will make this same argument, because they will hear something from one of our witnesses as to which they have a document they would like to impeach the witness on, and they would not like us complaining that they hadn't turned it over. So it works both ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may just briefly respond -- MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just to what Mr. Ackerman has said, the prosecution, in fact, agrees with Mr. Ackerman that there are going to be situations where a witness testifies unexpectedly and a document may become relevant that was not previously deemed to be relevant. That's understood and of course there will be such situations, and as long as the prosecution believes that that is the issue, that, in fact, someone in good faith did not believe it was going to be used in evidence, and then something unexpected happens such that it became relevant, the prosecution does not intend to object. That is not the case here. Also just with respect to Mr. Ackerman let me just make it clear: the discovery rules are continuing. So when the prosecution continues to get material, it provides it to the defence, and so the fact that we are giving them documents now, in fact, we think is evidence of our compliance with the discovery obligations. So just with respect to Mr. Ackerman, I don't, in fact, believe there's any disagreement between us. I think the interpretation between Ms. Residovic and I is -- MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I would just say that I'm very surprised and I expect my learned colleague McHenry to apologise for some of the words that she uttered before this Tribunal, that this is a mockery of this Trial Chamber, the way I'm trying to present my evidence. I think that I have spent enough time working this, and I don't think this is a proper way to describe the work of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. (Pause). MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): This is as regards the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are quite right, but nobody is making mockery of the Rules here, so you can forget about that expression.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. If anything I said -- I was not accusing Ms. Residovic of making a mockery out of this. I don't know if possibly there was even a translation -- I did use the word "mockery" but not to speak of Ms. Residovic, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually these parts of the answers which we have in Rules, it was not intended to operate the way in which it is being interpreted. Do you have anything to say? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, as you just said, Rule 66 that was invoked on 29th May of last year by the defence and has been complied with as ruled by the Trial Chamber with the different judges, I think that based on that this is not the right way to level an objection against us, and this does not regard only the documents that the Prosecutor intends to use as evidence, but also the evidence that the defence intends to use. So this obligation cannot be completely identified with Rule 67C. We do comply with it, but we have the right to use any document or statements and here the Rule does not speak of the statements. The Trial Chamber has ruled separately on it and we have been complying with that Ruling. We are able to use this either as an aide-memoire or to question the credibility of a witness or authenticate it. We have the right to approach a witness with it and only then do we decide whether we are going to use it in evidence or not. So that triggers off our secondary obligation of discovery.
