utterances.text: On 31st August I went back to Hangar Number 6, where I stayed until somewhere around the end of November, when I was transferred to a building. It was Number 22, which they called an infirmary, and I stayed there until December 9th, 1992, when I was transferred among the last 32 detainees to the Konjic Sports Hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Dordic. Now coming back to the very first day when you arrived at Celebici, that means May 30th, when you first entered Hangar Number 6 approximately how many prisoners did you observe being in Hangar 6 when you first arrived in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my estimate, about 100, maybe more. I couldn't count them, because I was in great suffering. About 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were any of these prisoners familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were they from Bradina as well, or from other villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some from Bradina and from Brdjani, from the Serb village of Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did any of these prisoners have traces of injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them. All the prisoners had been badly beaten up. They were black and blue. Some had already had some bandages. Some of them had band-aid on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally see any of them receiving any medical treatment right after your arrival in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see. In the evening of 30th Radoslav Vujicic was taken outside, probably because he was helping us when we asked for water. At that moment, we don't know who it was beat him up so badly that both his arms were broken. Then the next day Hazim Delic came and gave him some injections. I don't know what it was. He said: "Friend, who did this to you?" Because this Radoslav Vujicic had worked with Hazim Delic before. That's all that I remember seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sir, did the number of prisoners in Hangar 6 have any variation during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The numbers were increasing all the time, so that at one point there were about 250 of us. This was in June, July, somewhere until 21st August, so that it ranged. About ten days later the number went up to about 250.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now describe the physical characteristics of this building, of Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate it must have been some kind of a garage. I don't know exactly how long and how wide it was, but about 25 metres by 12, something like that. There was a concrete floor. There were metal sheets on the sides and a metal roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there -- was there a door or more than one door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one side of the hangar there were those big doors like accordion along the whole wall of one side and then at the end of the other there was a small door that opened outwards, and that was the door that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there any windows in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, did any prisoner have a given position inside the hangar, inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was Hazim Delic who told each one of us where we would sit. We all had to sit there folded with our knees up, our arms on our knees, and to look down for a time, and then later when he walked in, we all had to get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So, your Honour, may I ask, please, that the witness be provided with the photocopy of the prosecution Exhibit Number 1, page seven, the map that we have used already many times, please. May the usher place it in the ELMO? Mr. Dordic, if you look at this piece of paper, can you recognise this map as the map of Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you indicate the door of the hangar on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- all this was a door and this was the small door (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Using this map, can you please show to the court how were the prisoners distributed inside Number 6? I mean, how were their positions organised inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating). There were about 100 of us and we were lined up like this, and later when the number increased to about 250, then there were another two rows across the middle here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally maintain the same position during the whole period of your stay inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you indicate on this map your position inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was fifth from the end here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you mark, please, with an "X" your position there so that we might --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere here, number five from the end. There was a pillar here and I was third from the pillar -- rather, fourth from the pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm asking you to sign an "X" there marking your position inside the hangar with a pen, please. May I ask the usher to give a pen to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where should I put a cross? Here, where the cross is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, may I tender this photocopy with the right position of the witness inside the hangar for admission? It should be Prosecution Exhibit number 15 ..

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: 157. Okay. Thank you. Now, Mr. Dordic, how were the general conditions of life in Hangar Number 6? I mean, food, drinking water, etc., and sleeping facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food was very bad. We got something twice a day and it consisted of each time a slice of bread. One loaf was shared into 14 or 18 pieces. Two or three spoonfuls of some kind of vegetable. Then there were periods when we received nothing and this was from 13th-17th July, when we got no food at all, and we prisoners from Bradina were not even given water. The water was also distributed two or three times a day. One bottle was shared by about seven or eight people, depending on how many people there were between the pillars that supported the structure. We were lucky if the bottle happened to be one of a litre and a half rather than a litre. As far sleeping facility, we slept on the concrete floor. If anyone had a jacket or something to put beneath him. Our shoes served as a pillow. We couldn't look after our hygiene at all. We washed very rarely. For toilet needs the time was fixed. We were taken out twice a day for urination. If you wanted to go to the toilet for some other reason, you had to ask the guards, but that also depended on who was on duty. I know that Hazim Delic would force us to go to urinate in a group of 30-40 people. We had to run there. Upon his command he would say: "Take it out. Stop." This was very short, the time we had. We just ran out and had to run back, so that there were people who just didn't have enough time to finish. On one occasion when the Red Cross came -- I think the representative was Michel -- and he measured the time, and about 250 of us finished urination in less than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There was a toilet facility inside the hangar too, a container, or something, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a bucket. I don't know what it had been used for. We used it at night for -- to urinate in. We were taken out and we used a hole that had a plank across it, a board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, I think we have to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: At 10 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At 10 o'clock in the morning. (5.30 pm)
